subject: Chemistry
title: The Ozone Hole: CFCs Destroy a Shield
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The Ozone Hole: CFCs Destroy a Shield.

hook.text: In 1985, scientists found a hole in Earth's ozone layer over Antarctica. CFCs from spray cans and fridges had torn it open.

buildup.text: Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) were considered miracle chemicals—stable, non-toxic, perfect for refrigerants and aerosols.

discovery.text: UV light splits CFCs in the stratosphere, releasing chlorine. Each chlorine atom destroys up to 100,000 ozone molecules.

twist.text: DuPont initially denied CFCs were harmful. Rowland and Molina, who proved the link, were called alarmists—then won a Nobel.

climax.text: The Montreal Protocol of 1987 banned CFCs. The ozone layer is slowly healing and should fully recover by about 2066.

punchline.text: Miracle chemical, invisible destruction. One treaty is slowly healing the sky.

quiz.question: How do CFCs destroy the ozone layer?
options: UV light releases chlorine from CFCs, and each chlorine atom destroys thousands of ozone molecules
CFCs react with ozone to form toxic smog at ground level
CFCs absorb UV radiation that ozone normally blocks

details.summary: Chlorofluorocarbons released from aerosol sprays and refrigerants drifted into the stratosphere where UV light broke them apart, releasing chlorine atoms that catalytically destroyed ozone molecules..
details.whyItMatters: The ozone crisis and its successful resolution through the Montreal Protocol remain the greatest example of international cooperation to solve a chemical environmental threat.
takeaways: CFCs release chlorine that catalytically destroys ozone in the stratosphere
One chlorine atom can destroy over 100,000 ozone molecules
The Montreal Protocol phased out CFCs and the ozone layer is recovering

faq.question: How does one chlorine atom destroy so many ozone molecules?
faq.answer: Chlorine acts as a catalyst. It reacts with ozone to form chlorine monoxide and oxygen. The chlorine monoxide then reacts with another ozone molecule, releasing the chlorine atom again to repeat the cycle. One atom can destroy 100,000 ozone molecules before being deactivated.

faq.question: Is the ozone layer fully recovered yet?
faq.answer: Not yet, but it is on track. The Antarctic ozone hole is gradually shrinking and is projected to return to 1980 levels by approximately 2066. The Montreal Protocol is considered the most successful environmental treaty ever, proving that coordinated chemical regulation works.
